newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak Nafta rejects foreign sale reports.
newsitem.headline: Slovak Nafta rejects foreign sale reports.

text.p: Slovakia's oil and gas storage company Nafta a.s. Gbely on Tuesday dismissed as "ridiculous" press reports and comments by opposition politicians that the company might be sold to German or Russian investors.

Last month the opposition Social Democratic Party (SDSS) accused Nafta's majority owner Druha Obchodna a.s of trying to sell the firm to an unspecified German company, but failed to present evidence of the allegation.
Earlier this week, the Slovak investigative weekly Plus 7 Dni reported that Druha Obchoda was negotiating the sale of Nafta to the Russian natural gas conglomerate Gazprom.
"This is all ridiculous, neither the management, nor the company owners have been negotiating sale of Nafta," company spokesmam Jozef Lacko told Reuters.
"There are no plans to start such talks, neither with domestic, nor with foreign companies," he added.
Officials at Druha Obchodna were not immediately available for additional comment.

Nafta has been surrounded by controversy since last August, when the National Property Fund, the state privatisation agency, sold its 45.9 percent stake to the private and little-known Druha Obchodna for 500 million crowns, far below its market value of about 3.2 billion crowns.
The block sale implied an average price of about 400 crowns a share, while at the time of the sale Nafta shares stood at around 2,400 crowns on the Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE)
The share has been plagued by low liquidity since privatisation and its price has since fallen, closing at 1,700 crowns on Monday, up 10 from last Friday.
Brokers said however that the sale of a Nafta stake to a foreign investor would help its share price recover.

"It wouldn't matter whether the buyer is German or the Russian Gazprom.... the owner would at least be transparent and well known and this would definitely help improve the share's image," said Dusan Sykora of ING Barings.
Brokers have been complaining that Nafta's owners have so far disclosed little publicly about their long-term strategy with the firm.
An extraordinary shareholders meeting in December approved one billion crowns in investment for the next eight years to expand activities, including an oil exploitation project in Kazakhstan.
But analysts said the owners failed to show stronger commitment to the development of the company, and did not reveal specifics of the investment plan.
